Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Assessment summary from transcript:
  - 45-year-old female with 3–4 months of progressive palmar dryness, fissuring and soreness interfering with work; intermittent pruritus; occasional bleeding after scratching; systemic well and afebrile per history.
  - Occupational exposure: hotel housekeeping with frequent use of cleaning agents; reports often not wearing gloves; temporal relation to job change ~3–4 months ago.
  - History of type 2 diabetes (on metformin) and generalized dry skin on legs; attempted E45 emollient and oral antihistamine without improvement.
  - Management communicated in visit: avoidance of triggers (glove use), topical steroid cream prescribed (agent/dose/route/frequency not documented), stronger emollients advised to apply 3–4 times daily for 1–2 weeks, prescription to be sent to pharmacy, review in 1–2 weeks or sooner if worsening.
- Diagnostic reasoning consistent with transcript (from DDx):
  - Irritant contact dermatitis (occupational) — High likelihood: strong temporal and exposure history, palmar distribution, chronic fissuring, failure of simple emollient alone.
  - Allergic contact dermatitis — Moderate likelihood: exposure to multiple chemicals and pruritus supports possibility; requires further evaluation (e.g., patch testing) to confirm.
  - Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection) — Low–Moderate likelihood: chronicity and diabetes increase susceptibility; no characteristic lesion description or concurrent tinea pedis documented.
  - Other considerations from DDx (less likely given history): palmar psoriasis, diabetic xerosis contributing to severity, secondary bacterial infection if lesions become acutely more inflamed or purulent.
- Conflicts/unsupported suggestions:
  - No direct contradictions between transcript and DDx. No physical exam or investigations documented to confirm or exclude alternate diagnoses.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Irritant contact dermatitis (occupational) — High likelihood.
  - Justification: Onset ~3–4 months after new housekeeping job with frequent use of cleaning products and inconsistent glove use; palmar distribution, cracking, pain; failed simple emollient treatment; aligns with clinician impression in transcript.
- Allergic contact dermatitis — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Occupational exposures can cause delayed hypersensitivity; pruritus prominent; would require patch testing or specialist input to confirm.
- Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection) — Low–Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Chronic scaly fissured palmar dermatitis can be fungal and diabetes predisposes to fungal infection; no clinical features or tests documented to support or refute.
